significance.justification: A verified-true result would establish a form-(iii) relation—“this coupling is stronger for languages where honorifics are grammatically obligatory” and “the status signal leaks across languages”—together with the form-(ii) causal claim that a shared residual-stream “status direction” changes sycophancy, hedging, and refusal. This would establish both a behavioral phenomenon and a mechanism, fixing expectations about which language systems should produce larger deference effects and whether Japanese honorific framing should affect an English answer; sycophancy is already treated as a distinct model behavior in Perez et al. (2022) and Sharma et al. (2023), so identifying a linguistic causal contributor would inform its explanation. The negative branch would distinguish a shared, behaviorally active status representation from language-compartmentalized or epistemically inert encoding, although the qualifiers “largely shared” and “stronger” and the compound three-part hypothesis make a blanket false result less decisive. In the topic-substitution check, the generic question of shared versus language-specific multilingual mechanisms would not earn this score: the honorific-obligatoriness gradient, cross-language leakage, and causal link to three behaviors are claim-specific, but they remain one linguistic case rather than a general law of multilingual representation.

reach.justification: The claim names a reusable handle—the “shared status direction,” including the intervention to “ablate the direction to REMOVE honorific-induced sycophancy”—as well as a measurable coupling between “honorific obligatoriness” and behavioral shift. This can be ex ante because the status representation is present in the prompt and can be neutralized before the answer is generated, giving auditors or deployment practitioners an action window rather than merely explaining an observed failure. After per-model re-extraction, the conclusion still predicts an ordering—stronger coupling in grammatically obligatory honorific systems—and cross-lingual leakage, although it does not predict exact magnitudes and may require language-specific calibration; its asserted scope covers multilingual models and typologically diverse languages. The topic-substitution check supports an above-median score because deleting the specific status direction, leakage relation, and ablation handle leaves only the broad multilingual-representation topic and no comparable screening or mitigation tool.
